description: Hi, I'm Taha, first-year Math-CS student at FSR Rabat, Morocco. Astronaut monitoring is high-stakes work and I want to build something real. I bring solid Python for data/backend logic, plus Linux/systems experience for reliable software. Looking for: data viz/dashboard skills (Plotly/D3), biometric/sensor data handling, space medicine knowledge, and a strong presenter for judging.
summary:
Orbiter is a browser-based tool that analyzes astronaut exercise sessions using one ordinary camera and no wearables. Pose tracking runs in the browser, so no video leaves the device. From the pose data, Orbiter counts repetitions and measures joint range of motion, left/right symmetry, tempo, movement energy, torso lean and center-of-mass drift. It produces a session report with a readiness score and compares each session against the previous one.

It addresses the challenge by making exercise movement measurable and comparable over time without extra hardware. Tracking the trend in a crew member’s own movement quality could give an early signal that an exercise routine is or is not holding up. An optional AI review adds a written interpretation, using summary numbers only.

This matters because exercise is a core countermeasure on long missions, where mass, sensors and bandwidth are limited. Orbiter is a screening aid, not a clinical measurement, and it states what a single camera cannot measure.
details:
Orbiter is a browser-based tool that tracks how an astronaut's exercise movement changes across sessions, using a single ordinary camera and no wearables. Exercise countermeasures matter on long missions, and Orbiter explores whether a webcam can give a useful trend signal without extra sensors. It measures repetitions, joint range of motion, left/right symmetry, rep tempo, movement energy and smoothness, torso lean and center-of-mass drift. Because it measures the same way every session, it compares each session against the previous one. The point is change over time, not a one-off score.

Pose estimation uses Google MediaPipe Pose Landmarker (33 landmarks) and runs entirely in the browser. No video is uploaded or stored, and this can be checked in the browser's Network tab during a session. Joint angles are corrected for video aspect ratio. Whole-body center of mass uses Dempster segment coefficients. A self-calibrating state machine splits each rep into descent, pause and ascent, and reports tempo ratio and compensation faults. Each session gets a 0-100 readiness score, four pillar scores (range of motion, symmetry, tempo, spinal stability), a rep-by-rep table and a heuristic countermeasure assessment oriented around ISS ARED exercise.

There are two analysis modes. Mode 1 is algorithmic and runs locally. Mode 2 is optional: it sends summary telemetry, never video, for a flight-surgeon-style written review and follow-up Q&A. Reviewers can use the hosted AI option with no key or setup (the key stays server-side), or supply their own key for Gemini, OpenAI or a custom endpoint - a user key lives in the tab only and is never stored. A built-in offline engine covers the no-internet case. The only data stored is the last session's summary numbers in the browser's localStorage.

It is built with plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS, MediaPipe (WASM), and Node test suites covering joint geometry, rep counting, synthesis, AI-coach routing and an end-to-end simulated session. The app is a static site with no build step, hosted on Vercel, plus one small serverless function that proxies the optional hosted AI review so no key is ever exposed to the browser. A synthetic demo session and a real NASA ISS treadmill clip let reviewers try it without a camera.

The creative angle is turning a webcam into a longitudinal monitoring tool for a setting where sensors, mass and bandwidth are scarce. We also tried to make it honest about its measurements. Sessions under 15 s, or tracked less than half the time, are reported but not scored. Running mode is descriptive only and leaves out fields it cannot measure instead of showing favorable numbers. One 2D camera cannot measure load or true 3D joint angles, so Orbiter flags change against a person's own baseline and does not claim to be clinical or diagnostic.

Factors we considered: privacy (on-device processing), zero deployment risk for judging, keeping AI interpretation optional and clearly labeled as experimental, and being explicit about what a single camera cannot measure.
